newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU summit set to offer taste of things to come.
newsitem.headline: EU summit set to offer taste of things to come.

text.p: Europe's future and its fissures will be on display on Friday when European Union leaders begin a two-day summit in Dublin that will touch on nearly every major issue facing the 15-nation bloc.

From the single currency to fighting drugs, from enlargement into eastern Europe to the future of EU institutions, the summit agenda is firmly directed towards the huge challenges EU leaders have set for themselves at previous meetings.
"We must demonstrate a commitment to advance the political and economic health of the Union," John Bruton, Irish prime minister and summit host said in a letter to his coleagues on Wednesday.

The leaders do not actually have to take any firm decisions, but will be required to acknowledge the direction the bloc is heading -- including future relations after a single currency is introduced and a new EU treaty to be agreed in June 1997.

Before things can even get to that point, however, EU finance ministers will have to end a row between Germany, the bloc's paymaster, and the rest over how tough life will be once the single currency is introduced on January 1, 1999.
Bonn insists that the fiscal discipline required to qualify for the currency, the Euro, must not be allowed to slip once economic and monetary union (EMU) starts.

Numerous meetings, including one between French President Jacques Chirac and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, have so far failed to reach agreement on a post-EMU pact that sets strict rules and fines regarding future budget deficits.
This has forced the finance ministers to meet on Thursday afternoon in Dublin ahead of the summit.
Most officials say they believe agreement will be reached, allowing leaders to present a united front.
Bruton said such a move was necessary to give momentum to EMU to be achieved on time. But even with an agreement on a pact there are major stumbling blocks.
Germany fears its partners are prepared to fudge the tough criteria set for EMU in order to let in countries such as Italy and Spain with far weaker economies.

Britain, whose ruling Conservative party is torn apart by political divisions over Europe, will be the alert to make sure the other countries do not try to steer its economic policies if London opts out of the Euro, as it is allowed to do.

Prime Minister John Major is also expected to play Cassandra when it comes to the EU's new treaty, being written to allow the bloc to expand into eastern and central Europe to embrace 10 or more new members.

His government has made it clear that, while it can accept a draft treaty written by host Ireland as a report on the state of play in negotiations, it will eventually block many of the individual proposals in it.

European Commission President Jacques Santer on Wednesday criticised this stance, saying countries could not have it both ways. If they wanted new markets in an expanded Union, as Britain does, they had to accept reforms to make the bloc work.

London's partners are banking on a new British election, to be held by May, to provide a more EU-friendly government that will be able to bend on such things as veto rights and writing an employment chapter into the treaty.

The Irish draft shows the majority of countries are heading towards closer cooperation in crime fighting, joint employment policies, stronger foreign policy links and a true border-free Europe with common asylum and immigration policies.

It calls for the EU to create by 2001 a vast area of freedom, security and justice that ensures the free movement of people. This is an attention grabber, designed to show Europe's citizens that the bloc has meaning.
But the divisions are sharp here too. Britain refuses any notion of opening its borders or of agreeing joint asylum and immigration rules.
France and the Netherlands, which takes over as EU president on January 1, remain at odds over Dutch drugs policy, which Paris sees as flooding France with narcotics.
